prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy
for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep my opening first choice, B009, because it is the clearest clue from nature on the table: a diffuse flux of TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos, observed in 2013 and since confirmed through independent channels, the 2017 blazar coincidence, NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane evidence. It opened a new window on the sources of cosmic rays and has the existential reach I care about. I now pair it with B051 because the discussion has moved me. Optical lattice clocks are the most broadly supported candidate among the colleagues who know the field, with a clean magic-wavelength idea, independent confirmation in many national laboratories at 10^-18, and consequences for tests of constants, relativity and geodesy. Together the two parts give a prize that is discovery-driven in two distinct directions, an observational discovery about the cosmos and a measurement invention, and the union is exactly three people. B050 remains my strongest alternative. It has the broadest support in the room and a decisive theory-experiment story, but the attribution problem around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is real, and I would want expert reports before committing.
statement.case_against: The weakest point of my configuration is attribution on B009: a single-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, with DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA as precursors, will be hard to defend and may need a second name or an expert report that I cannot supply from memory. The source-identification evidence is also still only moderate in significance. For B051 the objection is overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-clock prize, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some will say the prize is early. Finally, pairing two unrelated parts may look like a convenience compromise rather than a judgment that both are the top two discoveries; B050 alone would be the cleaner prize if the committee is satisfied on credit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B051 first because optical lattice clocks are the clearest case of a new measurement capability changing what can be observed, with multiple independent clocks confirming 10^-18 performance and a compact Katori-Ye pair.
responses.response: I ranked B051 eighth, and I now think that was too low. The criterion of new measurement capability reaching new physics (geodesy, constants, dark-matter searches) is a discovery-oriented one, and the independent confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE and PTB satisfies my demand for evidence rather than elegance. I still disagree on one point. The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is more than a footnote, because the committee must show that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement and not a continuation of comb and ion-clock metrology. I am persuaded that it is distinct, since magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms changes the stability regime, but I would want the expert report to say so explicitly.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that B051 rests on a clean original idea, that magic-wavelength trapping lets atoms be confined without perturbing the clock transition, and that the field is mature, with the redefinition of the second relying on these clocks.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case, and on the open question she raises about whether to wait for the redefinition of the second I would not wait. The Nobel Prize recognizes the discovery, not the metrological bureaucracy, and the performance is already demonstrated in many laboratories. Where I would press her is the priority split: she says she wants to check the 2001-2003 papers, and so do I, because the attribution between Katori's proposal and the contributions of Lemonde, Ye and others is exactly where a two-person credit could be challenged. That belongs in the request to outside experts.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B050 first, as a clean theory-experiment story of Z2 topological insulators with Kane and Mele predicting and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment confirming, mature and overdue rather than premature, with the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as the unresolved issue.
responses.response: We largely agree on the science, and I ranked it second myself. My qualification is on attribution. Calling the trio defensible but not unambiguous understates it for me: the HgTe route was the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Zhang's death means we cannot recognize him, which makes a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize look like it skipped the idea that Molenkamp tested. I also think the 2016 topological-phase prize is a larger overlap than she suggests. For these reasons I would put B050 as the first alternative rather than the lead, but I would not be upset if the committee prefers it, and the breadth of support for it deserves respect.

responses.point: Pearce shares my first place for B009, valuing instrument-driven physics, a firmly established diffuse flux, and recognizing that the single-name credit is workable only if the committee can justify a one-person award given the collaboration scale.
responses.response: I share his reading of maturity, and his remark that this is the physics he values is also how I see it. His caution about attribution is the point I most want to build on. Only Halzen is credited, so the committee has to ask not only whether he deserves it but whether naming him alone misstates how the discovery happened, and the credited-name set does not let us add anyone. I would support B009 as a prize part only if the expert reports confirm that Halzen's conception and leadership are what the community regards as decisive. If they do not, the right response is to drop B009 and fall back to B050, not to widen the credit artificially.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B038 (circuit QED) first, as the architecture underlying superconducting processors, regards it as distinct from the 2025 prize, and openly notes that he directs a national programme built on this architecture and may need to recuse himself.
responses.response: I respect the frank disclosure and I think it must be handled formally, with Johansson stepping back from the discussion and vote on B038. On the science I disagree with him on timing. Circuit QED is important, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is so close that I think the committee would be repeating itself, and the choice of three out of four names (Blais or Girvin on the theory side, Wallraff against Schoelkopf) is not resolved. I would keep it in view for later years rather than this one.

uncertainties: Whether outside experts will support a single-name credit for Halzen in B009, given the IceCube collaboration and the earlier DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA efforts.
Whether B051 will be read as a distinct achievement from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, and the exact priority split between Katori and Ye.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission makes B050 unworkable, or whether the committee accepts a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize.
Whether two unrelated parts are better than a single-discovery prize this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My Uppsala position, my PhD supervisor David Gross, and my collaborator Thomas Van Riet are not connected to any shortlisted credited names. I note that Johansson disclosed a possible conflict on B038.
